stem:
The diagram shows a parallelogram $ABCD$.
$E$ is the point on $DC$ such that $AE$ bisects angle $DAB$.
Angle $ABC = 116^\circ$.
figure_description: A plane-geometry figure, no axes, no grid. Parallelogram ABCD drawn with AB as the horizontal base and the figure leaning to the right, so that the angle at A is acute and the angle at B is obtuse. Use these coordinates (units arbitrary, keep the proportions): A = (0, 0), B = (9, 0), D = (2.19, 4.49), C = (11.19, 4.49). So AB = DC = 9 units and AD = BC = 5 units — DC is clearly longer than AD. E lies on side DC, between D and C, at E = (7.19, 4.49) (that is DE = 5 units, EC = 4 units, so E sits about five-ninths of the way from D to C). Draw the four sides AB, BC, CD, DA and the single segment AE. Label the vertices in capital italics: A at the bottom-left outside the figure, B at the bottom-right outside, C at the top-right outside, D at the top-left outside, E just above the top side DC. Mark the given angle only: a small arc inside the parallelogram at B between BA and BC, labelled 116° (with the degree sign). Draw NOTHING else: no arc or label at A, D, C or E, no equal-length tick marks on AD and DE, no bisector arcs on angle DAB, no 32°, 64°, 148° or any other angle value, no lengths, no right-angle marks, no 'not to scale' note.
solution:
(a) In a parallelogram, adjacent angles are supplementary (co-interior angles, $AD \parallel BC$).
Angle $DAB = 180^\circ - 116^\circ = 64^\circ$
$AE$ bisects angle $DAB$, so angle $DAE = \frac{1}{2} \times 64^\circ = 32^\circ$.

(b) Angle $EAB = 32^\circ$ (the other half of the bisected angle).
Since $DC \parallel AB$, angle $DEA = $ angle $EAB = 32^\circ$ (alternate angles).
Angle $AEC = 180^\circ - 32^\circ = 148^\circ$ (angles on a straight line, $DEC$).

Alternative for (b): angle $ADE = $ angle $ABC = 116^\circ$ (opposite angles of a parallelogram), so in triangle $ADE$ angle $AED = 180^\circ - 116^\circ - 32^\circ = 32^\circ$, giving angle $AEC = 148^\circ$.

(Setter's check of the figure: triangle $ADE$ has angle $DAE = $ angle $DEA = 32^\circ$, so $DE = DA = 5$ units; with $DC = 9$ units, $E$ lies strictly between $D$ and $C$, as drawn.)
syllabus_check: 4052 Angles, triangles and polygons: angle properties of parallel lines (co-interior and alternate angles) and of a parallelogram (adjacent angles supplementary, opposite angles equal), angles on a straight line, an angle bisector. Set from a diagram as SEAB sets this type: the parallelogram, the point $E$ on $DC$, the segment $AE$ and the given $116^\circ$ are shown; nothing to be found is printed. Marks 1 + 2 = 3 match the slot.
originality_note: A new configuration: a parallelogram with one angle bisected and the bisector meeting the opposite side, ending at the obtuse angle on that side. It is not an isosceles triangle with a point on a side, not a trapezium with angles in a ratio, not a circumcentre argument and not a circle; the given angle ($116^\circ$) and the chain $64 \to 32 \to 148$ are the setter's own. No context, so it clashes with nothing else in the paper.
